articles.title_orig: China opens training center with Laos, marking third overseas military base
articles.title_zh: China opens training center with Laos, marking third overseas military base
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE — China has announced the opening of a new airbase in Laos, described as a joint training center but marking its third overseas military base, and the second in Southeast Asia.
China’s Ministry of National Defense (MND) said on social media that the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport in Laos and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy started operation s today.
“The establishment and operation of the two institutions reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, aligning with domestic laws of both countries, as well as international law and common practices,” the MND said the announcement.
The new post, the MND said, is “not directed against any third party and aim to help further deepen practical cooperation between the two militaries and contribute to maintaining peace and stability in the region.”
The People’s Liberation Army currently operates a military facility at Djibouti in East Africa that opened in 2017, as well as a naval facility at Ream in Cambodia .
The MND added that the new facility, located at Ban Keun some 25 miles (40 kilometres) north of the Laotian capital Vientiane, would be jointly operated and maintained by both countries and used to train Laotian pilots.
A video posted by the MND said that the opening ceremony was attended by Laotian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Khamlieng Outhakayson.
Based on satellite photos on Google Earth, the new airbase appears to have been built partially over the location of an airfield previously known as Lima Site 44, one of a network of airfields and other outposts built in Laos by the US military and Central Intelligence Agency during the Vietnam War, according to Rice, Refugees and Rooftops , a 15-volume book by former Air America helicopter pilot Harry Richard Casterlin .
The Google Earth photos showed the runway in the early stages of construction in January, however lower-resolution satellite photos of the base from imagery firm Sentinel Hub taken on September 22 showed an approximately 2,000 meter (6,560-foot) runway has been built, with an aircraft parking apron and five hangars at the north end of the base.

The co-pilot of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has been arrested after seemingly attempting to crash the plane after stabbing the pilot, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday.
Passengers helped on-duty Flydubai crew, who were travelling on the flight, break into the cockpit and hold down the co-pilot, allowing the other pilots to safely land the plane ​in Saudi Arabia, according to Netanyahu. Saudi authorities will now interrogate ⁠the co-pilot of the flight in question, FZ1073.
“During the flight, as they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and, apparently, tried to crash the plane with its passengers on board,” Netanyahu said in a statement released by his office.
“I spoke with one of the Israeli passengers, he told me that the plane went into a spin and began to descend,” Netanyahu continued. “He told me that, somehow, he managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members and, together, they overpowered the pilot who had carried out the stabbing.”
Flightradar24 data showed the aircraft plunged nearly 14,000 feet within 30 seconds during the incident.
Netanyahu praised the actions of those who intervened, calling them “heroes” who had “demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness” and “saved many lives.”
Flydubai issued a statement confirming the aircraft had been "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight” and relaying that all passengers and crew are safe and accounted for.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” the airline added.

articles.title_orig: Here’s The White House’s 308-Word AI ‘Accord’ In Full—Including Misspelling
articles.title_zh: Here’s The White House’s 308-Word AI ‘Accord’ In Full—Including Misspelling
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI
The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday.
At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”.
It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents.
Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control.
Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth.
Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social , and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed.
The Bloomberg News correspondent David Gura appeared to be the first to notice the spelling error.
The Guardian has asked the White House for comment
The accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”.
Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.
External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI.
The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September.
Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI. A recent New York Times/Siena College poll found that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while an SSRS/CNN poll found that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI.
While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected.
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.”
The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.

articles.content_orig:
The British government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident over the weekend at the RAF Fairford air base in England, which has been used by U.S. warplanes carrying out strikes on Iran, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday.
Burnham's remarks to the BBC were the first confirmation by the British government of its assessment of the incident, which saw five men — all British nationals in their mid-20s — arrested near RAF Fairford early Sunday morning on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. They were all released on bail the following day , however, even though the police had the right to hold them for up to 14 days under U.K. counterterrorism laws.
Their quick release drew criticism from President Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But it also prompted questions in the U.K. as to whether the authorities had overreacted.
Top Lebanese officials, including President Nawaf Salam and Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi, met with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Wednesday to discuss reclaiming land from the Iran-backed Hezbollah militia.
"The discussion focused on the government's efforts to restore Lebanon's sovereignty and extend state authority across its entire territory, as well as progress on reforms and economic recovery," Raggi said in a statement .
Sens. Jim Risch, Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons and Tim Kaine met with the Lebanese leaders.
Hezbollah has grown in power and political influence in Lebanon since the 1990s and consistently launched operations against Israel. The group launched strikes into Israel in March in the wake of Israeli and U.S. attacks on Iran.
As part of a trilateral agreement signed between the U.S., Israel and Lebanon in late June, official Lebanese forces were supposed to progressively take over security from Israel, which invaded southern Lebanon in response to the strikes from Hezbollah. Israel, however, has resisted, saying it needs Hezbollah to completely disarm beforehand.
Iraqi armed factions backed by Tehran said Wednesday they were "not bound by any timeline or agreement" to surrender their weapons to the state, as the government seeks to disarm them under mounting U.S. pressure.
A military spokesman for Kataeb Hezbollah, Jaafar al-Husseini, said at an event to celebrate the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces that the factions had been in talks on "regulating" their weapons but "have not yet received a response from the Iraqi government."
"Based on this, the Islamic Resistance declares that it is not bound by any timetable or agreement that any governmental or political party has spoken of or may speak of," al-Husseini said.
The U.S. military announced on Wednesday it had officially pulled out of Iraq after 12 years fighting the Islamic State. The U.S. and Iraqi government had agreed to a pullout by Sept. 30 and began the process over recent months.
The militias in Iraq have launched attacks on other Gulf countries in the wake of the U.S. and Israeli launching war on Iran in February. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia launched joint strikes on those militias in late July.
A British maritime agency said Wednesday that unknown projectiles struck three ships in the Strait of Hormuz the previous day. A crude oil tanker and two other vessels had each "been struck by an unknown projectile," the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said.
It had earlier described one of the vessels as an LNG tanker, before later describing it as a tanker.
The Strait of Hormuz is at the center of the war between Iran and the United States.
Around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passed through the strategic shipping lane before the war. But since the conflict broke out, Tehran has been attempting to block the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorized crossings.
Washington has responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting its oil.
An Iranian woman sentenced to death over protests earlier this year has begged the international community to save her life and those of others facing the death penalty, according to an audio message she sent from prison that was shared Wednesday by rights groups.
The plea by Mahboubeh Shahbani, 33, from a prison in the eastern Iranian city of Mashhad, came after authorities executed two more men on charges linked to the major anti-regime protests in January.
Rights groups accuse Iran of ramping up executions of high-profile prisoners in a bid to intimidate the population and ensure there is no repeat of the protests, which preceded the U.S. and Israel launching their joint war against the Islamic republic on Feb. 28.
Iran more than doubled its use of executions in 2025 , Amnesty International said earlier this year.
"The sentence handed down to me shows that many others are in danger of execution," Shahbani said in a telephone call from the phone for prisoners in Mashhad's Vakilabad prison.
"I am not worried about myself. I am worried for the others whose sentences have been upheld," she said in the call, an audio recording of which was shared by Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) and the U.S.-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
It was not immediately possible to verify the authenticity of the message.
"I call on everyone - the public, the U.N., human rights organizations. Not just for me but for all the others whose sentences have been upheld and who have spent months sleeping in fear and stress at night," she said. "I call on them to do something."
According to the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), Shahbani was convicted of carrying out actions "to strengthen Israel, the U.S., and individuals affiliated with opposition groups" in the protests.
IHR said she had merely used her motorcycle to transport injured protesters.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said lasting security in the Persian Gulf and its waterways depends primarily on cooperation among, and is the responsibility of regional countries, in a message marking World Maritime Day.
"The Strait of Hormuz, as one of the most important maritime passages, has a special position in the security and economy of the region and the world," Pezeshkian said, according to Iranian state news agency IRNA.
"Our approach to this strategic waterway is responsible and based on maintaining the security, stability and interests of the countries of the region," he said. "We believe that lasting security in the Persian Gulf and its waterways depends, more than anything else, on the cooperation, responsibility and role of the countries of the region."
Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. regional allies around the Gulf since the war began in late February, as well as commercial vessels it accuses of attempting to navigate the Strait of Hormuz without its permission.
Iran's semi-official Fars news agency claimed Wednesday that Iranian security agencies had received intelligence suggesting Israeli plans to orchestrate a false-flag "mass-casualty incident" to blame on the Islamic Republic.
Fars, which is linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said intelligence obtained by an Iranian security agency pointed to a scenario it said had been proposed by the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad to the prime minister's office involving an operation against aircraft or airports in the region.
The report claimed the plan was to "create a mass-casualty incident and provide the grounds for attributing responsibility for it to Iran."
Fars reported separately on the FlyDubai incident Wednesday that saw a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent cockpit altercation, which some reports suggested could have started as an attempted hijacking by one crewmember. The Iranian news agency did not link the FlyDubai incident to the purported intelligence about a possible Israeli false-flag operation.

Chad Lowe, the brother of fellow actor Rob Lowe, won an Emmy Award in 1993 for TV show Life Goes On and has appeared in other programmes including Pretty Little Liars and Supergirl.

articles.title_orig: Project B picks China as first stop for new women's basketball tour
articles.title_zh: Project B picks China as first stop for new women's basketball tour
articles.content_orig:
Project B is going to China in 2027, the women's basketball league announced on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province, will the first stop on the Project B's inaugural circuit. The league plans to play at the Hangzhou Olympic Sports AT Center Gymnasium from Jan. 19–24. The league announced the news with help from co-founder and chief strategy officer Russell Westbrook, co-founder and chief basketball officer Alana Beard and Chinese basketball player Li Meng.
“China has always had incredible energy around basketball, and I’ve experienced that personally throughout my career,” Westbrook said via release. “Project B is connecting basketball with culture in each place we play. I have deep respect for the history and tradition here, and also the constant drive to create what comes next. This combination is powerful.”
Training camp and Project B's first draft will be in Seoul from Jan. 6-12 ahead of players arriving in Hangzhou. The league's first season will then begin the following week. Additional details about the Hangzhou stop are expected to be announced at a later date.
“From a basketball perspective, we wanted our first stop to set the standard,” Beard said. “We’re bringing the best players in the world together to compete at the highest level, and we’re also creating an environment where they can experience new cultures and build real connections with fans. Starting in Hangzhou gives us an incredible stage for both.”
Project B's women's basketball league has more than 20 WNBA players who have signed on, including Azzi Fudd and Alanna Smith of the Dallas Wings, Alyssa Thomas of the Mercury, Awa Fam of the Seattle Storm, Jewell Loyd of the Las Vegas Aces, Jonquel Jones of the New York Liberty, Kamilla Cardoso of the Chicago Sky, Kelsey Mitchell and Sophie Cunningham of the Fever and Nneka Ogwumike , who retired from the WNBA at the end of the season.
The concept for Project B is to have two separate leagues ― men and women ― with six teams, each with 11 players. Those teams will compete in a global circuit slated to kick off in Jan. 2027 and run through April 2027. Each city will host a 10-day event, crowning a city champion, and those victories will count towards a season-long championship. Project B has revealed that, outside of Hangzhou, it will also play in Tokyo, Japan and Valencia, Spain.
Athletes who play in Project B are expected to have equity in the league. Project B hasn’t disclosed any salaries yet, but a league spokesperson previously told USA TODAY Sports they are “higher than anything you’ve ever seen in women’s sports."
The global basketball league has multiple investors, including women’s basketball legends Cheryl Miller, Candace Parker and Lauren Jackson and NFL Hall of Fame quarterback Steve Young. Additionally, Project B has secured Host Broadcast Services (HBS) to be the official broadcaster for the league’s inaugural circuit . HBS has broadcast the FIFA World Cup since 2002. The games will stream live on YouTube.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court has stayed the execution of Christa Gail Pike, the only woman on the state’s “death row”, US media reported on Wednesday.
Tennessee had been set to execute the first woman in more than 200 years on Wednesday, after the United States Supreme Court rejected a bid to halt it. However, the Sixth Circuit US Court of Appeals intervened at the last minute.
Christa Pike, 50, who was convicted of torturing and killing a classmate when she was 18, was due to die by lethal injection at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, but according to a report by The New York Post, she has asked to be shot by an all-female firing squad instead.
Human rights experts have condemned the decision to continue with the execution at all, but say the Supreme Court can still overturn the stay of execution.
Lawyer Clive Stafford Smith, who has represented many death row inmates in the past, told Al Jazeera: “Very few women are executed, but fewer still in Tennessee – it has been 200 years. So this is a step back to about 1820.
So why does Pike hope to avoid lethal injection in preference for the firing squad, and how does the US put people to death? Here’s what you need to know:
Pike was found guilty of the murder of another young woman she viewed as a romantic rival more than 30 years ago.
In January 1995, Pike, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson lured Colleen Slemmer, 19, into a wooded area and tortured and killed her. All four were students at a Job Corps vocational centre in Knoxville.
The case attracted huge public interest, especially after it was revealed that the attackers had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, which Shipp later admitted to carving. Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull.
Pike and Shipp confessed and were convicted of first-degree murder in 1996. Pike was sentenced to death; Shipp received life with the possibility of parole.
“Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions,” her lawyers wrote.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has spoken in support of the execution.
That she should not be executed at all.
On Wednesday, just hours before Pike’s execution was due to be carried out, a federal appeals court issued an order stating: “The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee determined that it did not have jurisdiction over Christa Pike’s Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(6) motion to reopen the judgment denying habeas relief. Therefore, it is ORDERED that execution of the sentence of death upon the movant is STAYED until further order of this court.”
However, the Supreme Court can still overturn this order, Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera. “The Supreme Court has been overturning stays recently,” he added.
Pike’s legal team previously petitioned the governor to commute her sentence to life without parole. It pointed to evidence that her mother drank heavily during pregnancy, impairing Pike’s brain development and her impulse control.
“The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists,” her lawyers wrote.
She would be the only person to be executed in modern-era Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
Her lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, said scientists now understand far more about adolescent brain development and that her sentence was an outlier.
Stafford Smith said: “Christa was just a teenager, and had undergone horrendous abuse as a child. Now she is 50, a totally different person. It is so pointless – will this really make the world a more civilised place?”
Governor Bill Lee has denied clemency, however. A group of United Nations human rights experts has called for her sentence to be commuted.
The US almost never executes women.
Women account for 18 of the 1,683 people executed since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976 – just more than 1 percent.
Tennessee has executed just 17 people in that time before Wednesday, with Pike the only woman on its death row.
If the execution goes ahead, it will be the state’s first execution of a woman since 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Her legal team and trauma experts say it could force her to relive abuse she suffered in childhood.
Her clemency petition documents childhood violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was aged 11 and 17. It also cites her diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Sexual violence and trauma experts argue that the procedures around lethal injection would likely trigger severe flashbacks of that abuse.
Her legal team also argues that she has small veins and a blood condition that could make it difficult to place an IV line, a claim the state disputes.
In May, Tennessee prison officials abandoned the execution of another prisoner, Tony Carruthers, after failing to find a suitable vein.
According to The New York Post, Pike’s lawyers said she also fears a painful death by lethal injection.
The paper reported that she wants to be shot by an all-female firing squad, with members of Slemmer’s family among the witnesses.
Tennessee is not among the five states that authorise the firing squad.
In court in August, her lawyers proposed hanging instead, noting it was the method Tennessee last used to execute a woman.
The state opposed that, saying Tennessee has neither the equipment nor the legal authority to carry it out. The judge sided with the state but allowed for the possibility of an all-female execution team.
Tennessee also allows prisoners whose crimes predate January 1999 to choose the electric chair; Pike’s crime took place in 1995.
There are 27 states with the death penalty, although four have placed its use on hold.
Lethal injection is authorised in every state with the death penalty; electrocution in nine states; gas in nine; and the firing squad in five. In Idaho, the firing squad became the primary method in July 2026.
Tennessee authorises lethal injection and electrocution. If both are found unconstitutional, its law allows any constitutional method.
Since 2008, the Supreme Court has required prisoners challenging an execution method to identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces the risk of severe pain.
In June, a federal judge permanently barred Alabama from executing Jeffery Lee with nitrogen gas, ruling that it violated the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
She found his proposed alternative, the firing squad, feasible.
The US has used five: lethal injection, electrocution, gas, the firing squad and hanging.
Lethal injection accounts for 1,491 executions since 1976, while electrocution has been used 163 times. Gas has been used 19 times, with Alabama and Louisiana the only states to have used it.
In nitrogen executions, a mask is placed over the prisoner’s face, and the air they breathe is replaced with pure nitrogen.
The firing squad, the method Pike reportedly wants, has been used just six times since 1976.
Hanging, once a primary method, is not currently authorised in any state.
Because none of them reliably work as intended, many experts say.
The Eighth Amendment to the US Constitution bars “cruel and unusual punishments”. But the Supreme Court has made challenges to the death penalty harder to win. It has ruled that proving a method risks severe pain is not enough; prisoners must also identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces that risk.
Lethal injection depends on finding a usable vein. If the drugs go into a muscle instead, or the needle clogs, the prisoner can suffer extreme pain.
In 2017, legal challenges in Arkansas cited botched lethal injections in Oklahoma and Arizona.
Meanwhile, the electric chair does not always kill with the first jolt. If the prisoner’s heart is still beating, another jolt must be applied.

articles.title_orig: MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research
articles.title_zh: MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research
articles.content_orig:
Security service says academics should stop taking grants from and working with firm backed by China’s intelligence service
MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
China’s intelligence service used a front company to pay grants to British universities and steal crucial research about technology projects, MI5 said on Wednesday in a rare public espionage warning.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 believes it poses a “significant threat”.
The Chinese organisation has given money to 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return getting access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
MI5 is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications, and the embedding of data in pictures online called steganography. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence. The Guardian understands that as well as research money, some British-based academics were given awards, as in honours, by the Chinese.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged cooperation.
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that the CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
It added: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
The alert warns of “potential criminal consequences”, in a section issued after consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service, which authorises criminal prosecutions in England and Wales.
“Through this espionage alert, MI5 has placed the fact that CGTRI has very strong ties to MSS in the public domain,” it states. “Going forward, academic institutions, staff and researchers should ensure they are aware of the National Security Act 2023, particularly offences under section 3 (assisting a foreign intelligence service) and section 17 (obtaining a material benefit from a foreign intelligence service).
“Under section 3, an offence is committed if the person a) engages in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities, and b) knows, or having regard to other matters known to them ought reasonably to know, that their conduct is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities.”
Such is the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK that MI5 has decided on a deterrence strategy via a public alert such as this, rather than pursuing every single case. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with the CGTRI.
The Guardian understands MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access to cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (searching and retaining useful information from social media sites).
The National Security and Investment Act 2021 could prevent a state such as China, assessed as having hostile intent towards the UK, from buying access to the technology on a commercial basis.
after newsletter promotion
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
He added: “International partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face. That means supporting our police and intelligence services to expose and disrupt harmful activity, using the full force of the law.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
“Close engagement between government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks.”
Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said: “All our universities take national security responsibilities very seriously. Working closely with government departments and the security services enables universities to take swift action to protect UK interests – and we will continue to do so in the face of new and emerging threats”.
The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike's execution temporarily halted, as Tennessee seeks to put to death first woman in 200 years
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike's execution temporarily halted, as Tennessee seeks to put to death first woman in 200 years
articles.content_orig:
A United States district court has temporarily stayed the execution of Christa Pike , the only woman on Tennessee's death row, just hours before she was scheduled to receive a lethal injection on Wednesday.
Although the execution has been halted, it could still proceed later Wednesday, an attorney for Pike said, as the state quickly asked the U.S. Supreme Court to override the last-minute district court order. If it does happen, Pike would become the only woman executed in Tennessee in the last 200 years.
"We will continue to advocate for the lawfully-imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue," said Phil Buehler, a spokesperson for Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti, who submitted the request to the Supreme Court. CBS News has also reached out to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
In granting the stay, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled that a "short" pause on the execution proceedings was needed in order to resolve new claims from Pike's legal team, which argued that counsel in her initial criminal case failed to properly introduce her extensive childhood experiences with abuse into their defense and was therefore ineffective.
Pike was supposed to be put to death at 10 a.m. local time Wednesday at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
"I am not afraid to die. I'm only nervous about the process," wrote Pike earlier this week, in a letter she penned before Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee denied her clemency petition and cleared the way for her execution to take place.
Thanking those who rallied for the governor to intervene and halt the plan, Pike said she was "at peace," regardless of the outcome of her bid. CBS News obtained a copy of the letter from her spiritual adviser, Rev. Mikey Noechel, along with a copy of another note Noechel received from Pike that contained handwritten lines from the poem "To ——" by Edgar Allan Poe. Noechel said he received the poem on Sunday and the letter on Monday.
Now 50, Pike has been incarcerated since 1995 for the murder that year of her former classmate, Colleen Slemmer. According to court records, Pike and Slemmer were students at the Job Corps Center in Knoxville when Pike, then 18, tortured and killed her, allegedly over comments Slemmer, 19, had made about her relationship.
Pike's boyfriend and another friend helped carry out the attack and murder, the records said.
Pike's case has drawn international attention and some outcry, with the United Nations recently joining local advocacy groups in their calls for Lee to commute her death sentence .
Their criticisms mainly center on the childhood abuse and untreated mental illness from which Pike suffered when Slemmer was killed, factors that play much larger roles in how juries make sentencing decisions now than they did at Pike's trial. U.N. experts also said the decades Pike spent in isolation on death row, as the sole woman awaiting execution in Tennessee, should amount to unlawful torture.
Once Lee announced the clemency bid had been rejected, Pike's attorneys issued a statement saying they were "deeply saddened and heartbroken" by the news. In it, they noted how much their client had changed while incarcerated.
"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," the statement said. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."
One of her attorneys, Luke Ihnen, told CBS News that "in her classic Christa way, she has spent her last days worried more about her friends, family and legal team than herself."
In a statement included with her clemency petition , Pike said she recognized that the ramifications of her crime have been "huge, unforgettable and ruined countless lives."
"It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected," she said. "I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
Prosecutors and jurors in Pike's initial criminal case, as well as the judges who presided over that trial and her numerous appeals, have often described Slemmer's murder as brutal and horrific. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told the Knoxville News-Sentinel after Pike's conviction in 1996 that she believed Pike was "evil," and the state "should kill her right away."
Records from Pike's trial show that Slemmer was repeatedly beaten and cut with both a meat cleaver and box cutter over the course of 30 minutes or an hour, in a wooded section of the University of Tennessee's campus.
When her body was found, a piece of the skull was missing and pentagrams had been carved into her forehead and chest, details that fueled a media firestorm and coincided with the "Satanic Panic" that swept the country in the '80s and '90s. Fellow students said Pike later bragged about the killing, revealing to one that she had removed and kept the missing piece of Slemmer's skull as a "souvenir."
Pike's boyfriend at the time of the killing, Tadaryl Shipp, and her friend, Shadolla Peterson, both helped her carry out Slemmer's murder, according to court records. Because Shipp was 17 at the time, he wasn't eligible for the death penalty and, instead, received a lifetime prison sentence. His parole was denied last year, but the case will be up for review again toward the end of 2031. Peterson faced probation, exclusively, in the wake of the murder after testifying against Pike at her trial.
Although Pike confessed to the crime, her legal team has filed numerous appeals challenging her death sentence and questioning whether she would still receive it if her case were tried today.
When Pike received her sentence at 20, in 1996, she was the youngest woman sent to death row in the United States' modern era of capital punishment. Now, she would be the only U.S. inmate put to death since that era began who was 18, 19 or 20 when their crimes were committed, if Wednesday's execution goes ahead. It would also mark Tennessee's first execution of a woman since at least 1820, according to research on the death penalty in early America.
Her attorneys have said Pike's history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect, as well as psychological conditions including PTSD, bipolar disorder and congenital brain damage, were not adequately represented in her original trial. They have also highlighted that, had Pike been just months younger at the time of the murder, she would not have been eligible to face capital punishment in Tennessee.
"In sentencing Pike to death, we rule out the possibility that her crime was a product of the immature mind of youth rather than fixed depravity," wrote U.S. Circuit Judge Jane Stranch in a concurring opinion on one of Pike's unsuccessful appeals in 2018. Despite siding with the majority's rule against her, Stranch acknowledged the controversy around Pike's death sentence, writing that "we presume that she is incapable of reform even though the stories of other teenage killers, many of whom have been rehabilitated behind bars, reveal other possibilities." Stranch also authored the order granting Pike's stay on Wednesday.
Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told CBS News last year that declining national support for capital punishment and the low rates of death sentences handed down to teenagers suggest Pike would have received a different sentence in contemporary times.
"Society's view of who is truly deserving of a death sentence has changed in the years since Christa Pike was sentenced," Maher said. "Her young age, mental illness, and the physical and mental abuse she suffered at the time of her crime would likely persuade a jury today she is not someone who should receive a death sentence."

Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.
On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The Guardian has reached out to the state department for comment on whether it had “blown” holds from Congress on releasing the funds due to concerns about their use.
Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).
Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa .
“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”
The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.
“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.
“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”
The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.
In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).
Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.
The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.
“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”
Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the state department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
ProPublica first reported that Trump officials had drawn up at least a dozen no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe and advocates for white South Africans.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.
A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.
A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.
One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.
And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.
The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. articles.title_orig: Spain, France align on welcoming UK back to EU, strengthening China trade defences
articles.title_zh: Spain, France align on welcoming UK back to EU, strengthening China trade defences
articles.content_orig:
French president, speaking alongside Spanish counterpart, Pedro Sánchez, says EU bid would be good news for UK and Europeans
UK politics live – latest updates
The French president, Emmanuel Macron , has reacted warmly to Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could rejoin the EU.
“Welcome back,” the French leader said in English with a smile. Speaking at a news conference in Madrid on Wednesday, Macron continued (in French): “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , said his country would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU.
The two leaders were responding to the British prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference in which Burnham said that Britain would not have a clear path “until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market” and that Brexit had “done more harm than good”.
In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said the government could maintain the status quo, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” for full EU membership.
Macron said the British had “always been useful in helping us simplify things” when the UK was part of the EU and were “demanding partners”. Burnham “is right to have this boldness”, he added.
Earlier, Macron, who has frequently accused the proponents of Brexit of misleading the public , said Brexit had been “the biggest lie of the last 30 years”, pointing to shortfalls in promised economic growth and trade opportunities.
Sandro Gozi, an Italian Social Democrat, told the Guardian: “Burnham has finally swept away the so-called red lines that have constrained the debate on Britain’s relationship with Europe. That is a welcome and important step.”
The MEP, who co-chairs the EU-UK parliamentary partnership assembly, added: “Europe should respond with the same openness. We should be ready to turn the page and build a new EU-UK partnership, removing unnecessary barriers and restoring much closer economic and political cooperation.”
EU officials welcomed the change in tone but said it was up to the UK to define what it wanted from the future relationship. They have told their British counterparts that the UK is welcome to join the customs union or single market via membership of the European Economic Area.
In recent weeks Brussels has again mooted British membership of the customs union as the answer to the bloc’s Made in Europe policy , which could exclude British clean technology and electric vehicles from valuable European subsidy programmes and public contracts.
But EU officials also stress that joining the customs union would require full alignment with EU trade policy and tariffs. Single market membership means accepting free movement of people, alongside free movement of goods, services and capital.
More than 10 years after the Brexit vote, the EU remains attached to its red lines. A recent proposal from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, that Canada should become the EU’s first-ever associate member is not seen as a serious option for the UK (or even Canada). The idea is widely regarded by EU insiders as an ill-defined symbolic gesture, with no legal basis.
after newsletter promotion
The EU and UK are due to hold a summit in Brussels with a date in the second half of November expected to be announced in the coming days. The annual gathering was postponed after the resignation of Keir Starmer.
The Burnham government has made resolving Britain’s exclusion from Made in Europe a top priority, but several EU sources say the issue will not be settled at the summit as the EU is yet to agree its internal position on key legislative texts.
France is the staunchest opponent of opening Made in Europe to countries outside the EU, including the UK.
Macron pointed to the limits of the UK seeking close ties with the EU while remaining outside. “You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union, nor can you decide to take what suits you and leave the rest,” he said. “So, come back.”
A European Commission spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union . It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

articles.title_orig: Eli Lilly says closely watched combo obesity regimen boosts weight loss in mid-stage trial
articles.title_zh: Eli Lilly says closely watched combo obesity regimen boosts weight loss in mid-stage trial
articles.content_orig:
Eli Lilly on Wednesday said its experimental combination regimen showed greater weight loss than a high dose of its top-selling drug, tirzepatide, alone in a mid-stage trial on patients with obesity and Type 2 diabetes.
The combo therapy met the study's main goals in a population that typically struggles to lose weight. The results boost hopes that it could serve as an alternative blockbuster treatment option for people who didn't respond to or see the results they wanted on the current GLP-1 products on the market. Lilly said it plans to start Phase 3 trials on the regimen at the end of the year.
The combination treatment combines Lilly's experimental drug eloralintide, which targets amylin – a hormone in the pancreas involved in appetite and satiety – with a low dose of tirzepatide, the active ingredient in its obesity injection Zepbound and its diabetes counterpart Mounjaro.
Tirzepatide targets two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP. Lilly believes that hitting all three pathways, including amylin, can further reduce appetite and improve weight loss – and the combo drug did just that in the 48-week Phase 2 trial.
People taking the highest dose of the combo regimen lost up to 23.3% of their weight, or around 54 pounds, on average. That treatment combined 9 milligrams of the amylin drug and 15 milligrams of tirzepatide.
Meanwhile, patients taking only a 15-milligram dose of tirzepatide saw 14.8% weight loss, or 34.4 pounds, on average. Those who took eloralintide alone lost up to 12.3% of their weight, or 28.6 pounds, on average.
"Patients may not get what they need from a drug like tirzepatide," Ken Custer, president of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health, said in an interview. "They may not get what they need from a drug like a eloralintide on its own. The ability to combine them together and provide even greater weight loss – that's definitely one obvious" benefit of the new regimen.
The combo treatment also lowered a key measure of blood sugar levels – A1C – by up to 2.9% on average. Higher-dose tirzepatide reduced A1C by up to 2.4% on average, while the amylin drug lowered it by up to 1.4% on average.
Lilly may face more questions from investors and the medical community about how well patients tolerate and stay on the highly effective combination therapy.
More patients on the combo regimen – 10.8% to 27%, depending on the dose – discontinued treatment due to side effects compared to the 2.9% of people on tirzepatide alone in the trial.
Up to 10.8% of people on the amylin drug alone discontinued treatment due to side effects, compared to 16.7% with placebo.
Lilly said the side effects were more frequent in groups taking the combination regimen compared to tirzepatide or the amylin drug alone. The most common side effects of the combo therapy were gastrointestinal-related, generally mild or moderate in severity, and mainly occurred when patients increased doses in the trial.
But Custer cautioned against reading too much into the combo regimen's discontinuation rates in Phase 2. He noted that the highest dose of tirzepatide similarly showed elevated rates, around 25%, in a mid-stage trial back in 2018.
"It's probably not the best indicator of the tolerability of a medicine," Custer told CNBC. "We do things in Phase 1 and Phase 2 to test what the molecule can do from an efficacy perspective. We also learn from those studies about how we should administer them, and then we make changes. We do this every time."
Lilly plans to adjust the dosing regimens for the combo treatment in Phase 3 trials, "and we expect that we'll end up with a very favorable balance of efficacy and tolerability," Custer added.
Lilly is also planning to advance a co-formulation of the two drugs in Phase 3 trials, meaning that patients will only need to administer one injection with both tirzepatide and eloralintide.
Results were presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy. On Wednesday, Lilly said it plans to advance the combo product into Phase 3 studies by the end of 2026.
Ahead of the Phase 2 data, some analysts said the study positions Lilly's combination regimen as a direct comparison to Novo's next-generation obesity treatment CagriSema, which combines drugs targeting amylin and GLP-1.

MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities

The Chinese organisation has given money to 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return getting access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
MI5 is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications, and the embedding of data in pictures online called steganography. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence. The Guardian understands that as well as research money, some British-based academics were given awards, as in honours, by the Chinese.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged cooperation.
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that the CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
It added: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
The alert warns of “potential criminal consequences”, in a section issued after consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service, which authorises criminal prosecutions in England and Wales.
“Through this espionage alert, MI5 has placed the fact that CGTRI has very strong ties to MSS in the public domain,” it states. “Going forward, academic institutions, staff and researchers should ensure they are aware of the National Security Act 2023, particularly offences under section 3 (assisting a foreign intelligence service) and section 17 (obtaining a material benefit from a foreign intelligence service).
“Under section 3, an offence is committed if the person a) engages in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities, and b) knows, or having regard to other matters known to them ought reasonably to know, that their conduct is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities.”
Such is the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK that MI5 has decided on a deterrence strategy via a public alert such as this, rather than pursuing every single case. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with the CGTRI.
The Guardian understands MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access to cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (searching and retaining useful information from social media sites).
The National Security and Investment Act 2021 could prevent a state such as China, assessed as having hostile intent towards the UK, from buying access to the technology on a commercial basis.

“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
“Close engagement between government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks.”
Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said: “All our universities take national security responsibilities very seriously. Reviews for the film have been hugely mixed, with one noting that the role is indeed a bold one for Tom, given his decades-long reputation for big budget blockbusters.
The Daily Mail's Brian Viner leaned on the side of praise, as he awarded the film four stars, writing: 'I've already seen Digger twice, and enjoyed it much more the second time, knowing the twists from the start.
'First time round, I felt it got tangled in its own conceit and artifice, becoming not just baffling but self-indulgent.
'Nonetheless, this is bold and often brilliant film-making, with deserved whispers of Oscar nominations for Inarritu, Cruise and Goodman, and fabulous supporting performances from Ahmed, Sandra Huller and Jesse Plemons , not to mention an animatronic cat.'

Other critics to laud the film included the BBC's Nicholas Barber, who wrote in his four-star review: 'Personally, I loved it. Some of its excesses are, well, a bit too excessive, and most viewers will wish it was shorter.
'After about 90 minutes, you get tired of close-ups of Goodman yelling while snake-sized veins bulge out of his forehead.
'But when Cruise is clambering all over the set, delivering thunderous lectures on the oil industry, I couldn't help grinning at the gargantuan scale of his performance, the conviction of the script's grim environmental message, and Iñárritu's antic style.'
In The Telegraph , Robbie Collin branded Digger 'the most bonkers film of the year', writing: 'Digger itself exists in that perpetually uncertain state, and I'm not sure whether the debate it's having with itself about art's impotence in the face of catastrophe is one it can, or even wants to, resolve.
'But what a thrill to watch Iñárritu and Cruise hash it out with so much beauty, daring and extravagance.'
Amy Nicholson wrote in The LA Times : 'Tom Cruise has dangled from cliffs, skyscrapers and planes, but oil magnate Digger Rockwell is his riskiest role in eons.'
Collider also praised Cruise's 'bizarre but brilliant performance', adding: 'Without special effects or stunts, the veteran star holds your attention throughout, grandstanding in a way that feels like an Oscar moment both in its intention and its impact.'
However, many reviews were on the negative side, with The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw awarding the film just two stars.
With critics sharply divided over Digger, are you intrigued enough to see Tom Cruise's dramatic transformation for yourself?
The big budget black comedy was positioned as a major awards contender for the actor, as he underwent a dramatic transformation to take on the role of an eccentric oil tycoon
He wrote: 'As with Adam McKay's Don't Look Up, there may be a tacit consensus, understandable at some level, that at least we have a big mainstream movie which is talking about the biggest issue of our time, and we have a duty to suspend critical objection.
'Digger certainly resonates with Donald Trump's greedy urge to despoil the Arctic and everywhere else. Yet there is something glib and overblown here. This film finds itself in a postmodern hole. And what do you do when you're in a hole?'
Kevin Maher in The Times went further, and gave the film just one star while writing: 'There surely exists an alternate movie universe where Digger is played by an actual ''older'' actor, say Dustin Hoffman or Ben Kingsley, and in that universe that film is certainly more effective than this one.
'Cruise, instead, is in the unenviable position of being Digger's sole selling point and its fatal flaw.'
In his two-star review, Empire's Olly Richards wrote: 'Digger is a bumptious blowhard... Cruise emerges with a win, reminding us how riveting he can be as an actor, not just as a movie star.
'A role so oversized and absurd demands fearless commitment, which he certainly gives. The big swing is laudable. If only the film were more rewarding.'
Writing in Variety , Owen Gleiberman said: 'I'm not sure that 'Digger' is going to connect, because it's so full of itself — so top-heavy with importance.
'The movie cost north of $125 million to make, and that figure is not only too big to probably justify itself; it's a testament to the arrogance of the filmmakers - to the assumption that we'll turn out in droves for this ponderous absurdist lecture.'
David Rooney of The Hollywood Reporter wrote: 'I was reminded of colossal misfires like Damien Chazelle's Babylon and David O. Russell's Amsterdam, bloated movies by directors so drunk on their exalted reputations they forgot there was an audience to consider.'
In one particularly scathing review, The Boston Globe called Digger a 'turgid, unfunny, and borderline unwatchable 128 minute mess'.
Den of Geek wrote, '[Digger] forgets the statement must still work as anything more than a self-flagellating valediction from a movie star.'
William Bibbiani of The Wrap said: 'Digger is what happens when you give the week's worst Saturday Night Live sketch an inexplicably large budget and delusions of grandeur.'
Johnny Oleksinski in The New York Post called the film an 'insufferable slog', writing: 'The trouble with Iñárritu's pretentious frame story (sorry to be so vague) is that it causes us to not take about 90% of the movie seriously and to zone out for long stretches.
'There are no stakes to be found and no laughs to be had. There's certainly no point.'
In her two-star review, The Independent's Clarisse Loughrey said: 'As much as Digger has been sold on the promise that Cruise here is a revelation, there's no real inversion to speak of, merely a return to the kind of work he did (over two decades ago!) before his blockbuster action streak.
'Even his latex makeover seems reminiscent of his paunchy, balding Les Grossman in Tropic Thunder.'
In Indiewire , David Ehrlich said: 'The reason why Digger is a nobler and more rewarding failure than Birdman or Bardo is because it doesn't have to pretend that Digger Rockwell is a real person.
'He's a living cartoon who's exempted from the human foundation that was missing from those earlier films, and — for all of this movie's psych-outs and detours — that allows Iñárritu to address his existential crises with a greater directness and degree of relatability.'

articles.title_orig: Trump to begin sending $500 ACA refund checks to 1 million Americans
articles.title_zh: Trump to begin sending $500 ACA refund checks to 1 million Americans
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Wednesday started sending $500 refunds to Obamacare enrollees whom the White House said were overcharged for healthcare by the Biden administration.
The Treasury Department is releasing these refund checks to more than 950,000 Americans in 30 states, according to an administration official. Some families with more than one "affected person" will receive multiple $500 checks or direct deposits, the official said.
Recipients will also receive a letter dated Sept. 30 from President Donald Trump, which is being mailed starting Thursday, the official said.
"For years, the Biden Administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov," Trump writes in the letter, which CNBC viewed.
The White House announced earlier this month that it would begin issuing refunds in October.
Trump's letter describes the move as a way to "restore Affordability, protect your hard-earned money, and lower the Cost of Healthcare."
"You have paid into this flawed System, and now you are finally getting something back," Trump wrote.
The refunds come just over a month before the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trailing Democrats in national and battleground polls .
Affordability has become a core theme of the election cycle amid stubbornly high inflation and rising interest rates . The Iran war has raised gasoline and energy prices for households while surging yields for Treasury bonds have pushed up rates for consumers seeking mortgages and car loans .
The refunds for enrollees in Obamacare — an informal name for the Affordable Care Act — come as millions of households saw their health insurance premiums spike after ACA enhanced premium subsidies lapsed at the end of 2025 .
Those enhanced subsidies, which lowered health insurance premiums for ACA enrollees, disappeared after the Republican majority in Congress defeated Democrats' efforts to extend them.
Jonathan Oberlander, a professor of health policy and political science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told CNBC earlier this month that the policy is likely a form of "damage control" for the White House to distract from higher healthcare costs.
"This announcement is less about health policy and much more about the 2026 Congressional elections," he wrote. "It's part of a broader effort by President Trump to buy continued Republican control of the House and Senate via promises of direct government payments to voters."
Health policy experts said a $500 refund does little to offset ACA premiums that, in many cases, rose by several thousand dollars per year for enrollees who had previously received enhanced subsidies.
The 30 states that will receive the Obamacare refunds are: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming.
These states use the federal ACA exchange, while the others use their own state-run marketplace. The latter tend to be governed by Democrats, according to health policy experts.
The largest number of refunds will be issued in Texas and Florida, where 139,000 and 127,900 people will get refunds, respectively, according to federal data shared with CNBC.
The primary recipients of the refunds will be people whose income is over 400% of the federal poverty line, the Trump administration official said. That's roughly $63,000 for an individual and $129,000 for a family of four.
These individuals lost all federal premium assistance when the enhanced subsidies disappeared this year.
However, "some people" between 100% and 400% of the poverty line will also receive a refund, the official said.
The $500 refunds are being paid from a "surplus" of "user fees" collected by the Biden administration, according to the Trump administration official. The White House said these excessive charges had been passed on to consumers during the Biden era through higher health insurance premiums.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services collects user fees from health insurers who participate in the ACA marketplace. Under Obamacare, healthcare exchanges can collect user fees from insurance companies to help fund ACA marketplace operations.
The fees went up and down during the Biden administration in different years — and were at times lower during the Biden era than during the first Trump administration, Oberlander said.

The scandal engulfing Cornell University over a woman’s allegations that she was gang-raped at a fraternity house has caused some prospective students to shun the Ivy League school, college advisers warned.
A former student identified as Jane Doe sued Cornell and seven male fraternity members, alleging that she was drugged and sexually assaulted for hours in October 2024 at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. No arrests have been made in connection to the case, and the local district attorney has said he is reopening the case in light of the civil suit.
Cornell is under fire for its response to the allegations, and Doe has accused the school of failing to protect her or adequately punish those responsible.
Prominent college advisers told the New York Post that several high school students they work with have scrapped plans to apply to Cornell as a result.
“All seven of the college applicants we work with for 2027 who planned to apply Early Decision to Cornell have decided not to apply at all,” Amanda Uhry, the founder of Manhattan Private Schools Advisors, told the newspaper.
“The parents will not permit them to go after what happened,” Uhry said of the seven prospective college students she is advising. “Nobody’s thinking about [applying to] Cornell anymore.”
College consultant Christopher Rim of Command Education said his clients are “shocked” about how Cornell has handled the incident. His international clients are particularly worried and have asked him whether it’s “how all U.S. schools” handle serious allegations.
“Parents who live halfway around the world just want to know their kids are in a safe environment,” he said. “And that remains to be seen.”
At the time of the alleged assault, Doe was 20 years old and a member of a sorority on campus, according to the 101-page complaint filed September 14 in New York County Supreme Court.
The lawsuit alleges that Doe was intoxicated and visiting a friend at the frat house when two male students pressured her into snorting a substance they claimed was ketamine in October 2024.
Multiple male students arrived at the house throughout the night, and Doe was subjected to an hours-long assault by seven of them, according to the complaint.
The filing details graphic abuse including men snorting lines of ketamine off her body, moving her between rooms and continuing to rape and sexually assault her while she was incapacitated.
Doe reported the incident to the Cornell University Police Department three weeks later, and an internal Title IX investigation began in January 2025. However, Doe’s attorney Thomas Giuffra told The Independent that Cornell’s response was severely lacking.
Out of the seven male students named in the civil filing, two were expelled from the university, according to Doe’s legal team. The other students allegedly involved were said to have received lesser punishments, which reportedly included temporary suspensions, required workshops or essay-writing assignments.
Following the uproar over the case, New York prosecutors are reopening the investigation. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office is weighing whether to bring criminal charges related to the incident, but said the allegations in the civil complaint are “dramatically different” from the woman’s statement to police at the time.
Lawmakers and public figures have condemned the alleged perpetrators and the university, including actors Florence Pugh, Mariska Hargitay, Josh Gad and Hudson Williams.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had “serious questions about Cornell’s campus culture and its systems for prevention, reporting, and response” in a statement. New York Attorney General Letitia James is also reviewing the university’s response to the allegations.
Cornell issued a statement supporting the DA’s decision to reopen the case, and pushed back against allegations that the school “did not impose consequential punishments for those involved.”
“A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault,” said Kyle Kimble, Cornell’s vice president for university relations.
Attorneys representing the named fraternity members have vigorously denied the claims in the lawsuit.
For those affected by rape and sexual abuse, if you are in the United States, you can call Rainn on 800-656-HOPE (4673).
Rape Crisis also offers support. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk .
